channel.title: Comments on: Instinctive Free Will
channel.description: taoism, taoist thought, buddha, yoga, tai chi, shakuhachi

item.title: By: Carl Abbott
item.dc:creator: Carl Abbott
item.content:encoded:
Free will is the absence of control, letting go of the need for control, accepting that flowing with the Tao, one’s chosen path is always in harmony.

The idea of there being a “one’s chosen path” is an example of the illusion of free will. Believing that humans are free to choose anything is a comforting story we tell ourselves. In fact, we are not different from any other animal on earth. Ironically, we only think (imagine) that we are, and relentlessly fabricate narratives to ‘verify’ it.

On the other hand, if by “free will” you mean that all animals have this capacity, then I fully concur. Of course, that makes the ‘free’ aspect meaningless, which means it all come down to a will-to-live shared by living things.

However, in my experience cultures view free will as solely a human capacity. We merely think we are different, and dare I say, uniquely so. We really are not any more or less unique than any other animal… meaning each species is unique in its own way.

I assume this elitist view is driven by our illusion of self (ego). This would not be such a big deal if it weren’t for our disease, i.e., Realizing I don’t know is better; not knowing this knowing is disease.

item.title: By: Michael A. Lewis
item.dc:creator: Michael A. Lewis
item.description:
"Our thoughts of having free will are driven by an instinctive need to control our actions."
"Free will" is not control. Living spontaneously, one is free to do whatever arises of the moment.
Free will is the absence of control, letting go of the need for control, accepting that flowing with the Tao, one's chosen path is always in harmony.
Free will is the opposite of determinism, as living in the Tao is the opposite of control.
